name: cppcoro
baseline: concurrencpp (also HPX and libcoro thread-pool runtimes)
workload: Recursive fork-join coroutine benchmarks on 64 worker threads: skynet (100M tasks, forks x10), nqueens (forks up to x14) and fib(39) (forks x2), run with cppcoro's static_thread_pool; matmul(2048) is a tie.
claimed_speedup: Third-party table, absolute times in us: skynet 144907 (cppcoro) vs 12514888 (concurrencpp), 11965484 (HPX), 119686148 (libcoro); nqueens 162773 vs 8000700 / 3452638 / 33347402; fib(39) 269384 vs 20663744 / 10789290 / 238019884. Mean ratio to best 3.67x for cppcoro vs 258.19x concurrencpp, 186.81x HPX, 2513.96x libcoro. Derived from page data: cppcoro is about 86x, 49x and 77x faster than concurrencpp on skynet, nqueens and fib, and about 83x, 21x and 40x faster than HPX. It is slower than tbb (3.25x), taskflow (3.34x), libfork (1.18x) and TooManyCooks (1.32x) on the same table.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 21.1.7 Release, -O3 -march=native, C++20; benchmark linked against a high-performance allocator (cppcoro's CMake prefers mimalloc, then jemalloc, and does not use tcmalloc on Linux); code pinned to andreasbuhr/cppcoro commit f05170fbc71aaae06dc31e32812f1caba9525377.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7742 64-core, 64 worker threads (no SMT), Debian 13 Server, CPU boost enabled, schedutil governor
tradeoffs: Experimental library by its own description; no standard-coroutine-header support in upstream (uses std::experimental style on older compilers), Windows-oriented networking, cmake/cake build. Peak RSS on the fork-join benchmarks is about 134 MB (skynet, nqueens, fib) against 9-14 MB for tbb, taskflow, libfork and TooManyCooks, because the thread-pool runtime allocates a coroutine frame per task.
caveats: Neither the repo README nor any first-party page carries timings: the README makes only qualitative design claims (the static_thread_pool schedule() will not allocate memory in the common case; async_mutex is lock-free). The numbers come from the third-party tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks suite, which measures the maintained fork https://github.com/andreasbuhr/cppcoro (its README lists only build-system, CI and header/namespace-selection changes versus upstream; no performance changes are listed), not lewissbaker/cppcoro itself. The baselines it beats (concurrencpp, HPX, libcoro) are other coroutine runtimes, not the std::future/std::async baseline from the brief, and no std::async row exists. cppcoro loses to TBB, Taskflow, libfork and TooManyCooks on every fork-join benchmark and uses 10x the memory; in the io_socket_st TCP ping-pong row it is the slowest of four (524717 us vs libcoro 483074 us, Boost.Cobalt 393036 us, TooManyCooks 339340 us). The author of the suite also authors TooManyCooks (a competing runtime). Allocator differs per library (cppcoro mimalloc-first, libcoro tcmalloc-first); library versions of concurrencpp and HPX are not stated on the README page. The upstream repo is dormant since 2022-09-02, and the book lead calls it unmaintained.
found_via: seed record pass: https://github.com/lewissbaker/cppcoro README (no benchmarks), then WebSearch 'cppcoro benchmark compared std::async std::future coroutine task performance results' led to https://github.com/tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks (README, build_and_bench_all.py, cpp/cppcoro/CMakeLists.txt)

name: Easylogging++
workload: Time to write 1,000,000 short text lines ('message #N: This is some text for your pleasure') to a log file, split across 1, 10 or 100 threads that share an atomic counter; best of 3 runs; Easylogging++ file output with default logger, format '[%datetime]: %msg', large flush threshold, against glog LOG(INFO) to a log directory.
claimed_speedup: From the spdlog v0.16.3 README benchmark table (seconds, lower is better): 1 thread 0.975s (Easylogging++) vs 1.066s (glog), about 1.09x faster (derived from page data); 10 threads 2.857s vs 3.032s, about 1.06x faster (derived from page data); 100 threads 4.512s vs 1.139s, i.e. Easylogging++ about 4.0x slower than glog (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Makefile in gabime/spdlog v0.16.3 bench/: g++ (version not stated) -march=native -std=c++11 -pthread -O3 -flto -DNDEBUG, with Easylogging++ built using _ELPP_THREAD_SAFE and config bench/easyl.conf (TO_FILE true, TO_STANDARD_OUTPUT false, PERFORMANCE_TRACKING false, Log_Flush_Threshold 10485760).
tradeoffs: Single-header, many features (custom sinks, performance tracking, hierarchical loggers, macros that define global state, _INITIALIZE_EASYLOGGINGPP). Repo archived read-only on 2025-07-06; its own README now recommends spdlog for new projects. Heavy macro and global-state design.
caveats: Evidence is a competitor's benchmark (spdlog author) from about 2015-2016, with Easylogging++ and glog versions and the g++ version unstated and the Makefile pointing at a local checkout (-I../../easylogging/src/). Mixed result: Easylogging++ wins by 6-9% at 1 and 10 threads but loses about 4x at 100 threads. Both libraries write to file with mostly default buffering, so I/O settings are not tuned for either side. The project's own README says only 'Extremely fast' with no numbers, and its maintainer notes third-party benchmarks of limited setups (links g3log issue #73). That issue (https://github.com/KjellKod/g3log/issues/73, null sink, unstated units, no compiler or CPU) shows Easylogging++ 410,725 vs glog 402,970 for 1 thread string, but glog ahead at 4 threads (196,734 vs 127,895 without the option); this is directional and not used for the tier. spdlog itself is about 3x faster than either in the same table.
found_via: seed record pass: https://github.com/abumq/easyloggingpp README (qualitative claims only), then WebSearch 'easylogging++ benchmark vs glog g3log log entries per second results' pointed to spdlog's README benchmark table, opened at https://github.com/gabime/spdlog/blob/v0.16.3/README.md and bench/ sources at tag v0.16.3

name: libcoro
workload: io_socket_st: TCP ping-pong between a single-threaded client and single-threaded server, each on its own event loop, libcoro io_scheduler with process_tasks_inline against cppcoro io_service; channel: async MPMC queue, libcoro queue on thread_pool (mt config) against Boost.Cobalt channel on single-threaded Asio (st_asio config).
claimed_speedup: Third-party table (us, lower is better): io_socket_st libcoro 483074 vs cppcoro 524717, about 1.09x faster (derived from page data), though Boost.Cobalt (393036) and TooManyCooks (339340) are faster. channel: libcoro_mt 409967 vs cobalt_st_asio 910778, about 2.2x faster (derived from page data), TooManyCooks 390771 / 391661.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 21.1.7 Release, -O3 -march=native, C++23 for libcoro; libcoro pinned to commit 44d12235a218a93cf6ce462f67c06a1287901c54 with LIBCORO_FEATURE_NETWORKING ON and TLS OFF; linked against tcmalloc_minimal.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7742 64-core, 64 worker threads (no SMT), Debian 13 Server, CPU boost enabled, schedutil governor
tradeoffs: C++20 library (task, generator, event, latch, mutex, ring buffer, thread_pool, io_scheduler, TCP/TLS/DNS networking) that uses a mutex-and-condition-variable thread pool and per-task heap frames; ships Android test harness. Fork-join workloads hit very high peak RSS in the suite: skynet 14.66 GB, nqueens 5.03 GB, fib(39) 15.81 GB against 11-14 MB for TooManyCooks and TBB.
caveats: Weak result. The only wins are one 9% single-threaded socket row against cppcoro (itself the slowest of the four in that table) and one cross-configuration channel row (libcoro multi-threaded vs Boost.Cobalt single-threaded Asio, so not equal footing; TooManyCooks single-threaded Asio is also 1.00x). On the fork-join benchmarks libcoro is the slowest runtime tested: mean ratio 2513.96x (skynet 119686148 us, nqueens 33347402 us, fib(39) 238019884 us, matmul 374412 us) against cppcoro 3.67x. The brief baselines (hand-written coroutine task types, std::async/std::future) are not measured anywhere. libcoro's own README gives only server example runs without a baseline: ab TCP echo 110753.80 requests/s and wrk HTTP 200 OK 325778.99 requests/s with 2.96 ms mean latency, both on an Intel Core i7-9750H, so those are not comparisons. Repo test/bench.cpp times coroutine sync_wait, thread_pool and scheduler counters against a plain direct-call loop but publishes no results. The suite author also authors TooManyCooks (a competing runtime); allocator selection differs per library. The cppcoro rows measure the andreasbuhr/cppcoro fork.
found_via: seed record pass: https://github.com/jbaldwin/libcoro README (server example numbers, no baseline) and test/bench.cpp, then WebSearch 'github runtime benchmarks libcoro cppcoro concurrencpp tbb fib nqueens skynet results' led to https://github.com/tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks (README, cpp/libcoro/CMakeLists.txt, io_socket_st.cpp, channel.cpp)
